title: Shimon ben Kimchit
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: His mother Kimchit had seven sons, all of whom served as High Priest. Jerusalem Talmud Yoma, chapter 1 [supplied halakhah label ה״א״ד], and Vayikra Rabbah 20:12 and Bamidbar Rabbah 2:26 relate that Shimon ben Kimchit, then High Priest, once went out to speak with the king of the Arabs. A spurt of spittle from his mouth landed on his clothes and made him impure; his brother Yehudah entered and served as High Priest in his place. That same day their mother saw two of her sons as High Priest. Hyman attributes to the scholar Graetz the view that this was the man called Shimon HaTzaddik (volume 2 [supplied page string 22י17]). It is very easy for a historian to describe one person or another as “righteous,” Hyman argues, but for the Sages the matter is very weighty. Hyman insists: “We have only the Shimon HaTzaddik who lived in the time of Alexander of Macedon.”

notes.text: דה״י here means history-writing, not the biblical Chronicles. Graetz’s page string remains corrupted. The checked Bavli parallel names Yishmael, with Yeshvav or Yosef as replacement; Hyman’s Shimon and Yehudah are retained as his source’s different account.

No new primary scalar was returned. The earlier Bavli comparison naming Yishmael and Yeshvav/Yosef replacements is inherited, not freshly inspected, and does not replace Hyman’s Shimon/Yehudah. The source supplies שבעה seven, king of the Arabs, and the mother seeing TWO sons as HIGH PRIEST that SAME day; all repeated offices are retained. The mouth/pronoun in the spittle episode is not independently adjudicated. The anomalous וגבגס and Alexander מקרון are not proof of a particular letter repair. Yoma ה״א״ד and Graetz 22י17 remain unresolved supplied forms. דה״י means history-writing in this context, not biblical Chronicles. Hyman calls conferring the epithet righteous VERY EASY for historians but VERY WEIGHTY for the Sages, then insists on ONLY the Shimon HaTzaddik of Alexander of Macedon’s time. This strong historical argument is attributed, not softened or admitted as a new identity conclusion. All source holds remain.

The consulted Jerusalem Talmud Yoma, chapter 1, names Shimon and Yehudah and gives both an Arab-king reading and an editorial reading placing the encounter on the eve of Yom Kippur. Bamidbar Rabbah 2:26 and Vayikra Rabbah 20:11 in the consulted digital edition also name Shimon and Yehudah. The Bavli’s two accounts in Yoma 47a instead name Rabbi Yishmael, with Yeshvav and Yosef respectively. Hyman’s printed citation to Graetz gives volume II and the numerals 17–22. In the fourth edition of Geschichte der Juden, volume III, second half, pp. 738–742, Graetz treats Simon ben Kamitos under Valerius Gratus separately from Simon Kantheras, whom he proposes as a later Simon the Just. Hyman’s own attribution and rejection are retained.
